text: PepsiCo, Inc. is a leading global beverage and convenient food company that was incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. The company operates through seven reportable segments: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC). FLNA produces and sells branded convenient foods such as Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, and Tostitos, distributed through independent distributors and retailers, and also operates a joint venture with Strauss Group to market Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads. QFNA produces and sells cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods like Cap’n Crunch, Life cereal, Quaker grits, and Quaker oatmeal, sold to independent distributors and retailers. PBNA manufactures and markets beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Propel, operating its own bottling and distribution facilities and selling to authorized and independent bottlers. PBNA also produces ready-to-drink tea and coffee through joint ventures with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks, and manufactures licensed brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and Dole Food Company and Ocean Spray Cranberries. In 2022, PBNA began distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage owned by Boston Beer Company, and sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG), which operates across North America and Europe, with PepsiCo acting as the exclusive distributor for TBG’s portfolio in the U.S. for small-format and foodservice customers via chilled direct-store-delivery. LatAm markets and sells convenient food brands including Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Sabritas, and Tostitos, as well as Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Pepsi Black, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, and also distributes ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. Europe markets and sells convenient food brands such as Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, and Walkers, and Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, and Pepsi Max, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with some markets featuring in-house bottling and distribution, and also distributes SodaStream sparkling water makers and dairy products such as Agusha, Chudo, and Domik v Derevne, and ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. AMESA markets and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, and White Star, and Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with some markets featuring in-house operations, and also distributes ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. The company serves customers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories. The aggregate market value of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock held by nonaffiliates as of June 10, 2022, was $224.2 billion, based on the closing sale price on that date on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The number of shares of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock outstanding as of February 2, 2023, was 1,377,251,316. Securities registered under Section 12(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 include Common Stock (symbol PEP), and Senior Notes due in 2024 (PEP24), 2026 (PEP26), 2027 (PEP27), 2028 (PEP28 and PEP28a), 2029 (PEP29), 2031 (PEP31), 2032 (PEP32), 2033 (PEP33), 2034 (PEP34), 2039 (PEP39), and 2050 (PEP50), all listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC. The registrant is a well-known seasoned issuer, has filed all required reports during the preceding 12 months and for the past 90 days, has submitted electronically all required Interactive Data Files, is classified as a large accelerated filer, and has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The registrant is not a shell company. Portions of the Proxy Statement relating to PepsiCo, Inc.’s 2023 Annual Meeting of Shareholders are incorporated by reference into Part III of this Form 10-K.

PepsiCo retains a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG, which operates across North America and Europe. In the first quarter of 2022, PepsiCo sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while maintaining this 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG. In the United States, PepsiCo serves as the exclusive distributor for TBG’s portfolio of brands for small-format and foodservice customers with chilled direct-store-delivery (DSD). PepsiCo also began distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage manufactured and owned by the Boston Beer Company, and has licensed the use of the Hard MTN Dew trademark to Boston Beer Company, which has appointed PepsiCo as its distributor for this product. AMESA, in either independent capacity or in conjunction with third parties, makes, markets, distributes, and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, and White Star, as well as Quaker-branded convenient foods, and beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi. These products are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers, with AMESA operating its own bottling plants and distribution facilities in certain markets. AMESA also sells ready-to-drink tea products through an international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. APAC, similarly, makes, markets, distributes, and sells convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, along with Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, sold to authorized and independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers, and also sells ready-to-drink tea products through the same joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand. Products are distributed primarily through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse systems, distributor networks, and e-commerce platforms and mobile applications, depending on customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices. Key ingredients include aspartame, corn, corn sweeteners, flavorings, flour, juice concentrates, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar, vegetable and essential oils, and wheat, with water used in manufacturing. Packaging materials include polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polypropylene, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, and paperboard cartons. PepsiCo integrates recyclability into product development and supports recycled content, including recycled PET, in packaging. Fuel, electricity, and natural gas are essential commodities, and PepsiCo manages price fluctuations through fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivative instruments like swaps and futures. Supply risks are mitigated through purchases from multiple geographies and suppliers, and while price increases may or may not be passed on to customers, supply constraints due to the Ukraine conflict, the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation, adverse weather, supply chain disruptions, and labor shortages were experienced in 2022 and continued into fiscal 2023. PepsiCo maintains voluntary supply chain finance agreements with global financial institutions, allowing suppliers to sell their accounts receivable to these institutions, which had no material impact on business or financial results. PepsiCo owns numerous trademarks essential to its global operations, including Agusha, Amp Energy, Aquafina, Arto Lifewtr, Baja Blast, BaiCaoWei, Bare, Bokomo, bubly, Cap’n Crunch, Ceres, Cheetos, Chester’s, Chipsy, Chokis, Chudo, Cracker Jack, Crunchy, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Mug, Diet Pepsi, Diet 7UP (outside the U.S.), Domik v Derevne, Doritos, Driftwell, Duyvis, Elma Chips, Emperador, Evolve, Frito-Lay, Fritos, Fruktovy Sad, G2, Gamesa, Gatorade, Gatorade Fit, Gatorade Zero, Gatorlyte, Grandma’s, H2oh!, Hard MTN Dew, Health Warrior, Imunele, J7, Kas, Kurkure, Lay’s, Life, Lifewtr, Liquifruit, Lubimy, Manzanita Sol, Marias Gamesa, Matutano, Mirinda, Miss Vickie’s, Moirs, Mother’s, Mountain Dew, Mountain Dew Code Red, Mountain Dew Game Fuel, Mountain Dew Kickstart, Mountain Dew Zero Sugar, MTN Dew Energy, Mug, Munchies, Muscle Milk, Near East, Off the Eaten Path, Paso de los Toros, Pasta Roni, Pearl Milling Company, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, Pepsi Max, Pepsi Zero Sugar, PopCorners, Pronutro, Propel, Quaker, Quaker Chewy, Quaker Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni, Rockstar Energy, Rold Gold, Ruffles, Sabritas, Safari, Sakata, Saladitas Gamesa, San Carlos, Sandora, Santitas, Sasko, 7UP (outside the U.S.), 7UP Free (outside the U.S.), Sierra Mist, Sierra Mist Zero Sugar, Simba, Smartfood, Smith’s, Snack a Jacks, SoBe, SodaStream, Sonric’s, Spekko, Stacy’s, Starry, Sting, Stubborn Soda, SunChips, Toddy, Toddynho, Tostitos, V Water, Vesely Molochnik, Walkers, Weetbix, White Star, Ya, and Yachak. It also holds long-term licenses to use trademarks in certain markets, including Ocean Spray. PepsiCo distributes Celsius energy drinks and Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. brands such as Dr Pepper, Crush, and Schweppes. Joint ventures in which PepsiCo has an ownership interest either own or have rights to use trademarks such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks. PepsiCo grants exclusive contracts to independent bottlers for the sale and manufacturing of certain beverage products in specific geographic areas, providing rights to charge royalties for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina, and specifying required manufacturing processes. Financial incentives are provided to customers, including volume-based rebates, product placement fees, promotions, and displays for independent distributors and retailers, and bottler funding for independent bottlers to support consumer incentives, advertising, new product launches, and vending equipment placement. Changes in the retail landscape, including retail consolidation, growth in e-commerce and subscription services, integration of digital and physical operations, and expansion of hard discounters, have increased the importance of major customers. In 2022, sales to Walmart Inc. and its affiliates, including Sam’s Club, represented approximately 14% of consolidated net revenue across all divisions, including concentrate sales to independent bottlers used in finished goods sold to Walmart; the loss of this customer would have a material adverse effect on the FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA divisions. PepsiCo competes in highly competitive beverage and convenient food markets against international companies, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and micro brands sold via e-commerce or local retailers. The Coca-Cola Company is PepsiCo’s primary beverage competitor in many markets, including the U.S., where in 2022, PepsiCo and Coca-Cola represented approximately 20% and 21% of the U.S. liquid refreshment beverage category by retail sales, respectively. Coca-Cola holds a significant carbonated soft drink share advantage outside the U.S. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends such as health and wellness and sustainability, as well as e-commerce growth. Success depends on effective promotion, new product development and reformulations, production efficiency, technology integration, advertising, packaging, pricing, vending equipment, and brand protection. PepsiCo conducts global research and development focused on creating consumer-preferred products through new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; improving manufacturing processes to reduce cost and environmental impact; reducing added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat; offering functional ingredients like whole grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, and micronutrients; developing sustainable packaging, including recyclable, compostable, or biodegradable options; advancing marketing and dispensing equipment; expanding beyond-the-bottle offerings, such as for SodaStream; investing in artificial intelligence and data analytics; strengthening omnichannel capabilities, especially in e-commerce; and reducing environmental impact through water conservation and sustainable agricultural practices. Research centers are located in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States. PepsiCo’s operations are subject to various federal, state, and local laws in the U.S. and over 200 other countries, including the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Food Safety Modernization Act, Occupational Safety and Health Act, environmental protection laws, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, Federal Trade Commission Act, Lanham Act, competition and trade laws, employment laws, alcohol sale and distribution laws, data privacy regulations such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, customs and trade laws, and the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act. PepsiCo adheres to all applicable global laws and regulations.

PepsiCo is subject to a wide range of federal, state, and local laws and regulations that govern workplace health and safety, employment practices, environmental protection, competition, trade practices, product labeling, data privacy, and supply chain operations. These include the Equal Employment Opportunity Act, the National Labor Relations Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, the Federal Trade Commission Act, the Lanham Act, the Robinson-Patman Act, and the Clayton Act. The company also complies with laws related to the sale and distribution of alcohol, data privacy regulations such as the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (as modified by the California Privacy Rights Act), and international trade laws, including customs regulations, tariffs, and laws governing the import or export of products and ingredients. PepsiCo is required to comply with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. In addition, it is subject to state and local statutes such as Proposition 65 in California, which mandates warnings on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects if above a safe harbor level. The company also faces regulations outside the United States, including food safety laws, international trade, supply chain rules like the U.K. Modern Slavery Act, occupational health and safety, competition, anti-corruption (including the U.K. Bribery Act), and data privacy (such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation). Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is especially important due to PepsiCo’s competitive position in many jurisdictions. The company relies on legal and operational compliance programs, in-house and external legal counsel, and other experts to ensure adherence to global laws. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering imposing new or increased taxes on the manufacture, distribution, or sale of PepsiCo’s products, ingredients, or substances, with tax structures varying—some applying to all beverages, others to those with caloric sweeteners, and some using flat, graduated, or per-ounce/liter rates based on added sugar or specific ingredients. Additionally, product labeling, marketing, and sales restrictions are being introduced or considered, including warnings about ingredients, age restrictions, and geographic limitations on product availability. Regulations to increase recycling, reduce waste, or restrict packaging—such as deposit return systems, extended producer responsibility policies, or bans on single-use plastics and PFAS-containing packaging—are also in place or under consideration. PepsiCo is subject to U.S. and foreign environmental laws, including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, as well as similar laws abroad. Ongoing concerns about climate change, water scarcity, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics are expected to lead to new or stricter regulatory requirements, which the company addresses through internal environmental compliance programs and planned expenditures. While these costs have not materially impacted financial performance to date, future changes could adversely affect results. The company also faces environmental remediation and indemnification obligations from historical activities or acquisitions, which are not expected to have a material impact on capital expenditures, earnings, or competitive position. PepsiCo employs approximately 315,000 people worldwide as of December 31, 2022, including about 132,000 in the United States, and maintains good relations with employees through numerous collective bargaining agreements. Protecting employee safety and health is a top priority, with investments in technologies such as fleet telematics, distracted driving prevention, ergonomic solutions, and machine safety to reduce workplace injuries. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company implemented safety protocols, provided personal protective equipment, and enabled testing, and has also supported employees and communities in Ukraine through humanitarian aid. PepsiCo believes its culture of diversity, equity, and inclusion is a competitive advantage, with approximately 27% of its global workforce being female and 44% of management roles held by women as of December 31, 2022. About 48% of its U.S. workforce is racially/ethnically diverse, and 33% of U.S. managerial associates are racially/ethnically diverse. The Board has overseen appointments of seven globally diverse or female executives directly reporting to the Chief Executive Officer. The company supports associate development through global training programs, career development plans, mentoring, and in-house learning such as PEP U Degreed, with over 1 million training hours completed in 2022. PepsiCo files annual, quarterly, and current reports, proxy statements, and other disclosures with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and these filings are available on the SEC’s website and on its corporate website at http://www.pepsico.com. The company communicates material information through SEC filings, press releases, public conference calls, webcasts, and its corporate website, and encourages stakeholders to review this information. The information on the website is not incorporated into any SEC filings. The document also includes a section on risk factors, highlighting risks such as the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, which has caused supply chain disruptions, increased costs, reputational risks, and business interruptions, and could impact demand for products. Demand for PepsiCo’s products depends on its ability to anticipate and respond to evolving consumer trends, including preferences for product quality, packaging, nutrition, and health concerns, as well as shifts in demographics, e-commerce, and channel preferences. Pandemics, such as COVID-19, have influenced consumer behavior and demand. Any failure to adapt to changing consumer preferences or to respond effectively to trends can reduce demand, lead to inventory write-offs, and harm competitive positioning. Damage to the company’s reputation—due to ethical lapses, environmental or social issues, product safety concerns, advertising, or social media responses—can reduce consumer demand. Product recalls due to quality, safety, or labeling issues, including those involving allergens, contamination, or misbranding, can result in financial losses, inventory destruction, lost sales, and reputational damage, especially as the company expands into new categories like alcoholic beverages. Failure to maintain oversight can lead to litigation, investigations, fines, or criminal liability. PepsiCo competes with international beverage and food companies, regional brands, private labels, and e-commerce-based microbrands, primarily on brand loyalty, taste, price, innovation, distribution, and marketing. The company’s ability to compete effectively depends on its capacity to promote existing products, launch new ones, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, and respond to consumer trends.

Our business can be adversely affected by a range of factors, including fines, penalties, damages, or criminal liability, particularly if consumers lose confidence in product quality, safety, or integrity—regardless of whether such concerns relate directly to our products. We face competition from international beverage and convenient food companies, regional and local manufacturers, private label and economy brands, and smaller firms selling micro brands directly to consumers via e-commerce or locally focused retailers. In many countries, including the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is our primary competitor. We compete based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and our ability to anticipate and respond to consumer preferences. Failure to effectively promote or develop existing products, introduce or market new ones, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, strengthen digital marketing capabilities, or respond to supply disruptions, pricing pressure (including from commodity inflation), or competitive actions—such as aggressive spending by rivals—can harm our business. We may also struggle to grow or maintain sales or category share, requiring increased capital, marketing, or other expenditures. Our success depends on attracting, developing, and retaining a highly skilled and diverse workforce, as employees are highly sought after by competitors, and labor market challenges such as wage inflation, labor shortages, employee turnover, shifts to remote work, and ineffective succession planning—especially for leadership roles like the Chief Executive Officer—can erode our competitive edge, increase costs, and damage our reputation. Water scarcity poses a significant risk, as we and our partners use water in manufacturing and raw material production; shortages, regulatory pressures, climate change, or conservation efforts can disrupt supply chains, increase compliance and production costs, lead to facility shutdowns or relocations, impair our water use goals, and harm our reputation. Changes in the retail landscape—such as growth in e-commerce and hard discounters—can negatively impact us if we fail to maintain relationships with these channels or traditional retailers, especially as key customers like Walmart increase their e-commerce presence. Consolidation among large retailers or buying groups reduces our competitive ability and weakens smaller customers’ purchasing power, potentially leading to lost orders or reduced sales. Disruptions in manufacturing or supply chains, including rising costs for commodities, packaging, transportation, labor, and other inputs—due to civil unrest, political instability, supplier constraints, seasonal shortages, natural disasters, pandemics, strikes, tariffs, port congestion, or cybersecurity incidents—can increase costs and interrupt product supply. Political and social conditions, including election outcomes, government shutdowns, hostilities, protests, and climate-related events, can create uncertainty in regulations, affect demand, and disrupt operations. Our ability to grow in developing and emerging markets—such as Mexico, the Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, and India—is uncertain due to competition, cultural differences, distribution challenges, economic instability, inflation, currency fluctuations, foreign ownership restrictions, nationalization risks, trade barriers, and complex compliance requirements, including under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the U.K. Bribery Act, and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. Adverse economic conditions, such as inflation, interest rate changes, tax shifts, recessions, volatile commodity markets, credit contraction, or currency devaluation, can negatively impact our operations and those of our business partners. Cyber incidents, including cyberattacks, network outages, software failures, employee errors, or natural disasters—especially as remote work increases our IT vulnerability—can disrupt operations, compromise data, lead to financial losses, litigation, regulatory penalties, reputational damage, or employee morale issues. These risks extend to third-party providers, including suppliers and cloud service providers, who may introduce malware through software updates or compromised accounts, and whose systems may be exploited or fail, indirectly affecting our business. Although past cyber incidents have not materially impacted our operations, future events could do so. Despite significant investments in network security, disaster recovery, and employee training, there is no guarantee these measures will prevent all incidents, and insurance may not cover all losses or reputational harm. Finally, failure to successfully complete or manage strategic transactions—such as acquisitions, joint ventures, divestitures, or refranchisings—due to integration challenges, unmet synergies, regulatory hurdles, tax inefficiencies, or differing interests among partners can also harm our business.

Our ability to achieve the full expected returns, benefits, cost savings, or synergies from strategic transactions within the anticipated time frame or at all, including obtaining necessary consents, clearances, and approvals, is subject to significant risks. These risks include difficulties in integrating manufacturing, distribution, sales, accounting, financial reporting, and administrative support activities and information technology systems with our company, or challenges in separating such functions during divestitures; operating under new business models or in new categories or territories; motivating, recruiting, and retaining executives and key employees; conforming to controls and policies related to financial reporting, disclosure, data protection, cybersecurity, environmental compliance, health and safety, and anti-bribery laws; retaining existing customers and attracting new ones; managing tax costs or inefficiencies; maintaining good relations with divested or refranchised businesses in our supply or sales chain; offsetting revenue losses from divested brands or businesses; managing the impact of decisions or actions by joint venture partners with differing interests; and facing unanticipated problems or liabilities such as contingent liabilities or litigation. Poorly executed or poorly managed strategic transactions have in the past and could continue to harm our business. We rely on third-party service providers, including cloud data providers, for payroll processing, health and benefit administration, and certain finance and accounting functions. Failure by these providers to meet their contractual, regulatory, or other obligations, or our failure to adequately monitor their performance, can lead to inability to achieve expected cost savings or efficiencies, additional correction costs, business disruptions, systems performance degradation, processing inefficiencies, security breaches, incorrect or adverse financial reporting, litigation, claims, regulatory proceedings, fines, penalties, reputational damage, or negative employee morale—all of which can adversely affect our business. We are also implementing a multi-year phased business transformation to migrate financial processing systems to enterprise-wide solutions, which has led to and could continue to result in systems outages and operating inefficiencies. If we fail to allocate and manage the necessary resources to build and sustain the required IT infrastructure or fail to achieve expected benefits from this initiative, our business could be harmed. Climate change poses risks by increasing the frequency or severity of natural disasters, extreme weather, and disruptions to agricultural production, affecting the availability and pricing of key commodities like potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, and oranges. Increased regulatory focus on climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, energy policies, and sustainability—including single-use plastics—may introduce new or stricter legal and regulatory requirements, such as carbon pricing or revised labeling, leading to significant increased costs and investment needs. Failure to meet or properly report on environmental goals or to respond effectively to climate-related regulations can result in adverse publicity, reduced demand, reputational damage, or litigation. Strikes or work stoppages, due to inability to renew or enter into satisfactory collective bargaining agreements with employees or third parties involved in manufacturing, production, or distribution, can impair product supply, lead to lost sales, increased costs, and disrupt operational changes, all of which can harm our business. Our financial performance depends on our ability to implement productivity initiatives, such as shared business service models, to reduce costs and improve efficiency. However, these initiatives may cause business disruptions, management distraction, reduced morale, unexpected attrition, difficulty attracting or retaining key personnel, and negative publicity. If we fail to achieve expected savings, we may not realize anticipated benefits, negatively impacting financial performance. We conduct annual or more frequent impairment tests on goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets, and evaluate amortizable intangible assets, property, plant, and equipment for impairment when there is a significant change in operating or macroeconomic conditions. Deterioration in assumptions about competitive conditions, macroeconomic factors, or the weighted-average cost of capital can result in impairment charges, adversely affecting results of operations. Exchange rate fluctuations, due to inflation, monetary policies, currency controls, or restrictions, impact our financial performance because our consolidated financial statements are in U.S. dollars and we operate globally, paying for raw materials and ingredients in multiple currencies. A downgrade or potential downgrade of our credit ratings—based on factors such as cash generation, indebtedness, shareholder distributions, and broader economic or industry conditions—can increase borrowing costs, impair access to capital and credit markets, reduce liquidity, and limit our ability to access commercial paper at favorable rates, all of which can harm financial performance. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering new or increased taxes on our products, especially beverages, due to ingredients like sugar, with examples including Italy’s flat tax of EUR 10 cents per liter on all beverages effective January 1, 2023. These taxes can increase product costs, reduce consumption, and lead to negative publicity. Similarly, limitations on marketing or sale of our products—such as warning labels, age restrictions, or location bans—have been introduced in places like Brazil and Canada, and color-coded labeling is being considered, which may reduce consumption, cause negative publicity, or lead consumers to perceive our products as not meeting health needs. Laws and regulations regarding plastic or packaging materials—such as extended producer responsibility, plastic taxes, bans on single-use plastics or PFAS-containing packaging, bottle cap tethering, or recycling requirements—have been implemented or are under consideration in the EU, Peru, and U.S. states, increasing product costs, impacting demand, and requiring capital investments to reduce virgin plastic use, develop alternative packaging, or revise labeling. Failure to comply with personal data protection and privacy laws—such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, California Privacy Rights Act, Virginia, Colorado, Utah, Connecticut, EU’s GDPR, and China’s PIPL—creates significant compliance costs and challenges, with non-compliance leading to litigation, fines, reputational damage, and regulatory scrutiny. Increases in income tax rates, changes in tax laws, or disagreements with tax authorities can adversely affect financial performance, especially given global trends like the OECD’s proposed global minimum tax of 15% and EU adoption of such rules, which may not be adopted universally and could still negatively impact us. The increasingly complex global tax environment increases tax uncertainty, compliance costs, and the difficulty of resolving tax audits or disputes, which may result in outcomes different from historical provisions. We also face risks related to intellectual property, including failure to protect our ingredient formulas, trademarks, patents, trade secrets, or business processes, or allegations of infringing on others’ rights, which could lead to costly litigation, reputational harm, operational disruptions, injunctions, inventory write-offs, or restrictions on product development and sales. Our business is subject to numerous laws and regulations covering production, storage, distribution, sale, advertising, labeling, content (including genetically engineered ingredients), quality, safety, transportation, traceability, sourcing, packaging, disposal, recycling, employment, environmental, social, and governance matters, and data privacy. Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is especially critical due to our competitive position. New laws, changes in regulations, evolving enforcement priorities, or differing standards across markets can increase compliance and capital costs, necessitate product reformulation, or otherwise harm our business. Growing societal and governmental attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to expanded disclosure requirements, increasing the scope and complexity of reporting obligations. Additionally, entering new markets or categories, such as the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor, has introduced and may continue to introduce new regulatory and compliance challenges.

Social and governance matters, including climate change and data privacy and protection, are significant areas of focus for the company. In many jurisdictions, compliance with competition and antitrust laws and anti-corruption laws is particularly important due to the company’s competitive position. Changes in laws, regulatory requirements, or enforcement priorities, as well as differing or competing regulations across markets where products are made, manufactured, distributed, or sold, can lead to higher compliance costs, capital expenditures, and production costs, or necessitate product reformulation, which may negatively impact the business. Increased governmental and societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to and may continue to result in new laws and expanded disclosure requirements, increasing the scope and complexity of reporting obligations. The entry into new markets or categories, such as the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor, has resulted in and may continue to result in additional regulatory exposure and higher compliance costs. If one jurisdiction imposes new laws or regulations affecting the manufacture, distribution, or sale of products, other jurisdictions may follow. Failure to comply with such laws or regulations—or allegations thereof—can lead to criminal or civil investigations, enforcement actions, including document requests, fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement of profits, or activity restrictions, all of which can harm the business. Third-party studies, whether scientifically valid or not, claiming health implications from certain ingredients or packaging materials have resulted in and may continue to result in new taxes, regulations, or lawsuits that adversely affect the business. Potential liabilities from litigation, claims, legal or regulatory proceedings, inquiries, or investigations can negatively impact the business. The company and its subsidiaries are involved in various legal matters, including those related to advertising, marketing, product labels, ingredients, personal injury, property damage, intellectual property, privacy, employment, tax, insurance, environmental, social, and governance issues, and compliance with applicable laws. These matters are inherently uncertain, and there is no guarantee of successful defense or that the company’s assessment of materiality, potential losses, or reserves will match the ultimate outcomes. Responding to these matters, even if ultimately non-meritorious, requires significant expense and resource allocation and may damage the company’s reputation or brand image. Regarding unresolved staff comments, the company has received no written comments from the SEC staff regarding periodic or current reports issued 180 days or more before the end of the 2022 fiscal year that remain unresolved. The company’s principal executive office is in Purchase, New York, and its facilities in Plano, Texas, which it owns, are its most significant corporate properties. Each division uses manufacturing, processing, bottling, production plants, warehouses, distribution centers, storage facilities, offices, research and development facilities, and other facilities, either owned or leased. Significant properties by division include: a research and development facility in Plano, Texas (owned); a convenient food plant in Cedar Rapids, Iowa (owned); a research and development facility in Valhalla, New York (owned); a concentrate plant in Arlington, Texas (owned); a convenient food plant in Celaya, Mexico (owned); two convenient food plants in Vallejo, Mexico (owned); a convenient food plant in Leicester, United Kingdom (leased); a manufacturing plant in Lehavim, Israel (owned); a dairy plant in Moscow, Russia (owned); a convenient food plant in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (owned); a convenient food plant in Wuhan, China (owned); a shared service center in Winston Salem, North Carolina (leased); a concentrate plant in Colonia, Uruguay (owned); two concentrate plants in Cork, Ireland (owned); a concentrate plant in Singapore (owned); and a shared service center in Hyderabad, India (leased). The land for certain properties is leased. Most plants are owned or leased on a long-term basis. In addition to company-owned or leased properties, the company uses a distributed network of plants, warehouses, and distribution centers owned or leased by contract manufacturers, co-packers, strategic alliances, or joint ventures in which the company has an equity interest. PepsiCo closely monitors market risks, including the potential for additional impairments or write-offs, and evaluates actions to mitigate any adverse effects on future financial results. See Notes 1 and 4 to the consolidated financial statements for details on impairment charges recognized in the year ended December 31, 2022. The ongoing deadly conflict in Ukraine has contributed to global geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, with certain operations in Ukraine suspended. Sales of Pepsi-Cola and other global beverage brands, as well as discretionary capital investments and advertising and promotional activities in Russia, have been suspended, negatively impacting and potentially continuing to impact the business. Operations in Russia accounted for 5% and 4% of consolidated net revenue for the years ended December 31, 2022 and December 25, 2021, respectively. Russia represented 4% and 5% of consolidated assets, including 9% and 1% of consolidated cash and cash equivalents, and 32% and 35% of accumulated currency translation adjustment loss as of December 31, 2022 and December 25, 2021. Operations in Ukraine contributed 0.2% and 0.5% of consolidated net revenue for the same periods, and Ukraine accounted for 0.1% and 0.3% of consolidated assets as of those dates. The conflict has led to volatile commodity markets, supply chain disruptions, increased cyber risks, reputational risks, employee safety concerns, business disruptions including labor shortages, significant ruble volatility, credit market limitations, higher transportation, energy, packaging, and raw material costs, environmental, health, and safety risks, and additional sanctions, export controls, or regulations, including restrictions on fund transfers. The conflict could result in temporary or permanent asset loss or further impairment charges. The full extent of the impact on the business remains uncertain and depends on evolving factors such as the conflict’s duration and scope, regional instability, and financial and economic sanctions, export controls, and other legislation. PepsiCo continues to monitor the situation and assess actions to mitigate unfavorable impacts on future results. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering new or increased taxes or regulations on the manufacture, distribution, sale, packaging, ingredients, or recyclability of PepsiCo products or packaging. These vary in scope—some apply to all beverages, including non-caloric ones, while others target beverages with caloric sweeteners like sugar; some regulate packaging types (e.g., plastic), while others aim to improve sustainability, reduce waste, or restrict packaging use. PepsiCo sells a wide range of beverages and convenient foods in over 200 countries, with product profiles, revenue, and packaging differing by jurisdiction, making it difficult to predict the scope or impact of potential taxes, regulations, or limitations. These measures may affect PepsiCo and competitors differently. The company continues to monitor existing and proposed regulations and considers actions to mitigate any adverse effects, including advocating for alternative measures. The retail landscape remains disrupted by the growth of e-commerce, mobile commerce, subscription services, integration of physical and digital operations, and the international expansion of hard discounters. Consumers are increasingly shifting to e-commerce, online-to-offline, and other online purchasing, a trend accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. PepsiCo monitors these changes and seeks to strengthen its global e-commerce and digital capabilities, such as expanding its direct-to-consumer business, to effectively distribute products through all existing and emerging channels and mitigate negative impacts. PepsiCo employs an integrated risk management framework, with the Board overseeing key aspects of risk assessment and mitigation, including cybersecurity, food safety, sustainability, human capital, and supply chain risks. The Board receives regular updates on risks, including from management and external experts on macroeconomic trends, and reviews risk topics in detail. Specific Committees provide oversight: the Audit Committee reviews financial, compliance, and employee safety risks and meets with the Chief Compliance & Ethics Officer; the Compensation Committee evaluates employee compensation to prevent excessive risk-taking; the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee oversees governance and succession planning; and the Sustainability, Diversity and Public Policy Committee monitors sustainability, diversity, equity, inclusion, and public policy risks. The PepsiCo Risk Committee (PRC), composed of senior executives including the CEO, CFO, General Counsel, and sector leaders, identifies, assesses, prioritizes, and addresses top strategic, financial, operating, compliance, safety, and reputational risks and reports progress to the Board. Division and key market risk committees assess division- and country-specific risks. The Risk Management Office provides guidance, tools, and analytical support to the PRC and other committees, identifies risks, and facilitates communication with the Board and its Committees. Internal Audit evaluates key internal controls through periodic audits, and Compliance & Ethics and Law Departments lead compliance policies. The Disclosure Committee, including the General Counsel, Controller, and heads of Internal Audit, Financial Planning & Analysis, and Investor Relations, evaluates information from the risk management framework to monitor disclosure controls and procedures and assess potential risks for disclosure. PepsiCo is exposed to market risks from adverse changes in commodity prices, foreign exchange rates, and interest rates. It manages these risks through productivity initiatives, global purchasing programs, and hedging. Commodity derivatives had a total notional value of $1.8 billion as of December 31, 2022 and $1.6 billion as of December 25, 2021. A 10% decrease in underlying commodity prices at year-end 2022 would have reduced net unrealized gains by $176 million, offset by lower commodity purchase costs. Foreign exchange risks are significant, as operations outside the U.S. generated 43% of consolidated net revenue in 2022, with Mexico, Russia, Canada, China, the U.K., and South Africa accounting for approximately 23%. Unfavorable foreign exchange reduced net revenue growth by 3 percentage points in 2022, primarily due to declines in the Turkish lira, euro, Egyptian pound, British pound, and South African rand, partially offset by a stronger Russian ruble. A 10% unfavorable change in exchange rates would have decreased net unrealized gains by $298 million, offset by an inverse change in the underlying exposure. The total notional amount of net investment hedges for debt instruments was $2.9 billion as of December 31, 2022 and $2.1 billion as of December 25, 2021. Interest rate derivatives had a total notional value of $1.3 billion as of December 31, 2022 and $2.1 billion as of December 25, 2021. A 1-percentage-point increase in interest rates, assuming year-end 2022 investment levels and variable-rate debt, would have decreased net interest expense by $48 million due to higher cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments. Volume metrics, including unit volume growth, are key internal performance indicators used for strategic planning and business evaluation. Beginning in 2022, unit volume growth adjusts for acquisitions, divestitures, and structural changes, and excludes the impact of the 53rd reporting week. Beverage volume includes concentrate sold to independent bottlers and finished products sold under company-owned or licensed trademarks, including joint ventures, and is reported in concentrate shipments and equivalents (CSE) or bottler case sales (BCS), both converted to an 8-ounce-case metric. CSE and BCS are not equal due to seasonality, product launches, mix, and inventory practices. BCS is considered a better measure of consumer consumption. PBNA, LatAm, Europe, AMESA, and APAC, through joint ventures with Unilever, market and sell ready-to-drink tea under the Lipton brand; PBNA also markets and sells ready-to-drink coffee through a joint venture with Starbucks. Convenient food volume includes sales of convenient food products bearing company-owned or licensed trademarks by PepsiCo and its noncontrolled affiliates, measured in kilograms internationally and in kilograms in North America.

Consolidated net revenue in 2022 was $86,392 million, compared to $79,474 million in 2021, representing a 9% increase, while operating profit rose to $11,512 million from $11,162 million in 2021, a 3% growth, with operating margin declining 0.7 percentage points to 13.3% from 14.0%. Operating profit growth was driven by net revenue growth and productivity savings, partially offset by operating cost increases and a 42-percentage-point impact of higher commodity costs. The loss of net revenue from the Juice Transaction reduced operating profit growth by 3 percentage points and was partially offset by a 1-percentage-point contribution from the 53rd reporting week. Additional unfavorable impacts included a 13-percentage-point impairment charge related to indefinite-lived intangible assets due to increased weighted-average cost of capital and revised future financial performance, a 12-percentage-point charge from the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and a 6-percentage-point impairment charge on intangible assets, investments, and property, plant, and equipment due to brand repositioning or discontinuation. These were partially offset by a 29-percentage-point gain from the Juice Transaction. The operating margin decline was primarily due to impairment charges, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and brand portfolio impairments, partially offset by the Juice Transaction gain. In the first quarter of 2022, PepsiCo sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG, which operates in North America and Europe; in the U.S., PepsiCo serves as the exclusive distributor for TBG’s brands for small-format and foodservice customers with chilled DSD. PBNA, LatAm, Europe, AMESA, and APAC, either independently or with third parties, make, market, distribute, and sell ready-to-drink tea products through a joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand, and PBNA also makes, markets, distributes, and sells ready-to-drink coffee products through a joint venture with Starbucks. Convenient food volume is measured in kilograms internationally and pounds in North America; FLNA markets Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads through a joint venture with Strauss Group. Other pension and retiree medical benefits income decreased by $390 million due to higher settlement losses, net interest expense and other decreased by $924 million due to lower average debt balances, higher interest rates on cash balances, and losses on hedged investments, partially offset by a prior-year charge of $842 million related to cash tender offers. The annual tax rate declined to 16.1% from 21.8%, primarily due to the Juice Transaction and adjustments to reserves for uncertain tax positions from an IRS audit. Organic revenue growth is a non-GAAP measure; in 2022, FLNA reported a 19% net revenue increase, driven by effective net pricing and a 2-percentage-point contribution from the 53rd reporting week, with unit volume decreasing 1% due to declines in Sabra joint venture products and variety packs, partially offset by growth in Doritos and Popcorners; QFNA saw a 15% net revenue increase, with unit volume declining 3% due to declines in oatmeal, cereals, pancake syrups, and mixes, partially offset by growth in rice/pasta sides and bars; PBNA achieved a 4% net revenue increase, with unit volume growing slightly due to a 1% increase in NCB volume (driven by mid-single-digit growth in Gatorade) offset by a 1% decrease in CSD volume (due to a double-digit decline in energy portfolio), and a 9-percentage-point negative impact from the Juice Transaction; LatAm reported a 21% net revenue increase, with convenient foods unit volume growing 3.5% and beverage unit volume growing 6%, driven by growth in Argentina, with mid-single-digit growth in several countries; Europe had a 2% net revenue decline due to unfavorable foreign exchange (9 percentage points), organic volume decline, and a 4.5-percentage-point impact from the Juice Transaction, offset by effective net pricing; beverage unit volume declined 7% due to declines in Russia, Ukraine, and Germany, partially offset by growth in France; operating profit in Europe decreased 207% due to a 110-percentage-point impact from the Russia-Ukraine conflict, a 98-percentage-point impairment charge on SodaStream, a 20-percentage-point impairment charge on intangible assets due to discontinued or repositioned juice and dairy brands in Russia, and a 91-percentage-point impact from higher commodity costs, primarily packaging materials and raw materials, partially offset by a 23-percentage-point gain from the Juice Transaction.
